data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"Ownership-based allocation systematically suppresses cross-cutting explanations because it imposes a lineage-dependency tax on interdisciplinary inquiry; the local cost of borrowing a foreign programme's ontology exceeds the expected local gain, so rival programmes never interact productively.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the dominant lineage's ontology is genuinely complete (i.e., it already contains all possible explanatory resources), then forcing phenomena into it is not suppression but accuracy, and no cross-cutting explanations are being missed.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"If lineage-translational costs are negligible (e.g., all programmes share a common formal language), then ownership-based allocation does not suppress cross-cutting explanations because researchers can freely borrow without friction.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"If ownership is granted on the basis of explanatory novelty rather than lineage continuity, then the mechanism reverses: ownership-based allocation would reward cross-cutting explanations rather than suppress them.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the problem space is fully decomposable (i.e., all phenomena fall neatly into disjoint domains), then cross-cutting explanations do not exist to be suppressed, and ownership allocation is purely efficient.","eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Under ownership-based allocation, any successor artifact must inherit the parent's theoretical commitments and ontology. A researcher operating within lineage A who suspects a phenomenon is better explained by lineage B's framework faces a choice: either attempt to integrate B's ontology (incurring heavy translation costs, risking internal inconsistency, and likely losing ownership of the resulting artifact) or force the phenomenon into A's native ontology (cheaper, preserves ownership, but risks missing the cross-cutting explanation). Because allocation rewards lineage continuity, the expected payoff of the first option is systematically lower than the second. Cross-cutting explanations therefore require the alignment of incentives across lineages, which the ownership model structurally precludes. The suppression is not intentional but emergent: it arises from the fact that the unit of credit and the unit of explanation are mismatched.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
